lessons.title: Configuring a Claude Project: instructions plus knowledge
lessons.eli5: A Project is like a labelled binder for one job. On the cover is a sticky note that tells Claude how to behave for this job (the instructions), and inside are the papers it should read first (the knowledge). Every chat you start in that binder can see both, so you never have to explain the job again.
lessons.body:
## What a Project is

A **Project** in Claude is a self-contained workspace for one stream of work. It holds three things together:

| Part | What it is | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| **Project instructions** | Standing directions that apply to every chat in the project | Tone, audience, format, rules ("always answer in British English", "flag anything that needs legal sign-off") |
| **Project knowledge** | Documents, text and other files you add to the project's knowledge base | Background Claude should draw on: policies, style guides, product sheets, past reports |
| **Project chats** | The conversations you start inside the project | The actual work. Each one can see the instructions and the knowledge |

The point of a Project is **reuse**. If you find yourself pasting the same brief, the same style guide or the same "you are helping the HR team…" paragraph into chat after chat, that context belongs in a Project.

> The diagram in this lesson was drawn for a developer tool, but the idea carries over: **broad settings apply everywhere, narrower settings apply to one workspace**. Project instructions are the narrow layer — standing directions for the work in this one workspace.

## When a Project is (and is not) the right tool

| Situation | Best fit |
|---|---|
| One-off question, quick rewrite of an email | Ordinary chat |
| Weekly newsletter that must follow the brand guide every time | **Project** |
| Onboarding helper that answers questions from the employee handbook | **Project** |
| A multi-source investigation of a market | Research mode |
| A single polished document you will share or reuse | Artifact |

A useful test: *will I come back to this material and these rules more than a couple of times?* If yes, build a Project.

## Setting one up, step by step

1. **Create the project** and give it a clear name ("Q4 Customer Newsletter", not "Project 3"). Use the name and description to help *people* find and understand the project; put rules in the instructions field, not here.
2. **Write the project instructions.** Keep them to the essentials: who Claude is helping, who the audience is, the tone, the output format, and the few hard rules. (Lesson *Writing effective system-level instructions* covers this in depth.)
3. **Add curated knowledge.** Upload the files Claude should actually rely on — or connect a source such as Google Drive or Gmail — and remember that quality beats quantity (see below).
4. **Test it.** Start a chat and ask three or four questions you already know the answers to. Check that Claude follows the instructions and uses the right file.
5. **Share it if the work is shared.** On Team and Enterprise plans you can share a project with colleagues (see below).

## Curating knowledge: less, cleaner, current

Claude treats what you put in the knowledge base as trustworthy background. That makes curation your job.

- **Relevant only.** A newsletter project needs the brand guide, the product fact sheet and two good past issues. It does not need the whole marketing drive.
- **Current only.** Remove superseded versions. Two copies of a price list with different numbers will produce inconsistent answers.
- **Clearly named.** "Brand-Voice-Guide-2026.pdf" is easier for you and Claude to refer to than "final_v3_REAL.pdf". You can then write instructions such as "for tone, follow the Brand Voice Guide".
- **Authoritative.** Prefer the official policy over someone's summary of it.

### What happens when the knowledge base gets big

Claude can only consider a limited amount of text at once (its context window), and recall degrades as the amount of text grows — Anthropic's documentation calls this "context rot" and advises that curation matters more than capacity. With a large knowledge base, Claude may work in retrieval (RAG) fashion, searching the knowledge base and pulling in the most relevant parts instead of reading every file in full; exactly when that happens, and on which plans, changes over time, so check the Help Center. The practical lesson holds either way: **clear, well-organised, non-contradictory files** make the answers far more reliable.

## Sharing and permissions (Team and Enterprise)

On Team and Enterprise plans, a project can be shared with colleagues. Sharing usually separates people who can view and use the project from people who can change its setup; the exact options vary by plan, so check the Help Center. The rule of thumb: give **edit** access only to the people who own the project's accuracy. Everyone else gets **view**. That keeps the instructions and knowledge from drifting because many people tweak them.

## Projects and memory

Claude also has a memory feature (the certification's prep materials list Memory among the features to understand), but don't rely on it as a substitute for good project design. Keep unrelated work in separate projects so each one has a focused instruction set and knowledge base, and so context from one job doesn't bleed into another. How memory behaves across projects can change — check current documentation rather than assuming strict separation.

## Worked example: an HR policy helper

*Goal:* managers keep asking HR the same leave-policy questions.

- **Name:** "Manager Policy Q&A"
- **Knowledge:** the current Leave Policy, the Expenses Policy and the Remote Work Policy (official PDFs, current versions only).
- **Instructions (summary):** "You help line managers understand company HR policy. Answer only from the policy documents in this project. Quote the section you rely on. If the policies don't cover the question, say so and suggest contacting HR. Never give advice about a named employee's individual case."
- **Test:** ask about carry-over of annual leave (known answer), about a policy that doesn't exist (expect "not covered, contact HR"), and about a named employee (expect a polite refusal and redirect).
- **Sharing:** HR business partners get edit access; managers get view access.

Notice what the design does: the instructions handle **behaviour**, the knowledge handles **facts**, testing confirms both, and permissions protect them.

## Plan details change

Exact limits and availability — how many projects a plan allows, how much knowledge you can add, which features sit on which plan — change over time. Check the Help Center rather than memorising numbers. The exam tests judgment about *when and how* to use a Project, not plan trivia.
keyTakeaways: A Project bundles instructions (how to behave), knowledge (what to rely on) and its own chats, for recurring work on the same material.
Build a Project when you would otherwise repeat the same context or rules across many chats.
Curate knowledge: relevant, current, authoritative and clearly named files. Remove superseded versions.

Claude's context window is finite and recall degrades as text piles up, so curation beats capacity; large knowledge bases may be handled through retrieval (RAG), which still rewards clean, non-contradictory files.
For shared projects, default to view-level access and keep edit rights for the people who own accuracy.
Keep unrelated work in separate projects so instructions, knowledge and context stay focused instead of bleeding together.
examTips: If a stem describes someone pasting the same brief or style guide into every chat, the answer is almost always 'set up a Project with instructions and knowledge'.
When an option says 'upload everything so Claude has full context', prefer the option that uploads a curated, current set.
Instructions control behaviour, knowledge supplies facts. Pick the option that puts each in the right place.
For shared projects, the safest answer usually limits edit rights to owners and gives others view access.
commonTraps: Hiding rules in the project's name or description. Use those to help people find the project, and put standing rules in the instructions field.
Uploading old and new versions of the same document 'for completeness', which produces contradictory answers.
Using one giant project for unrelated work, which mixes knowledge and context that should stay separate.
Assuming a bigger knowledge base always gives better answers. Irrelevant or stale files make answers worse.
Giving every colleague edit access, so instructions drift as people tweak them.

lessons.title: Managing uploaded knowledge and connectors (Google Drive, Gmail and more)
lessons.eli5: Uploading a file is like handing Claude a photocopy: it stays frozen as of the day you copied it, so you have to swap in a new copy whenever things change. A connector is like giving Claude a key to the filing room: it can read the papers as they are today, but a key opens a lot of drawers, so only hand over the ones the job really needs.
lessons.body:
## Two ways to give Claude information

| | **Uploaded knowledge** | **Connector** |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | A file you add to a chat or a Project | A link between Claude and an outside service (the exam guide's own examples are Google Drive and Gmail) |
| Freshness | A **snapshot**. It stays as uploaded until you replace it | Reads from the **live service**, so you work with current content rather than a frozen copy |
| Scope | Only the files you chose | The data your connected account can reach in that service |
| Actions | Read only | Can **retrieve data and, for some connectors, take actions** |
| Who sets it up | Any user | You connect and sign in with your own account; plan settings and organisational policy control what is allowed |

Neither is 'better'. The skill the exam tests is **picking the right one for the situation and managing it responsibly**.

## When to upload, when to connect

- **Upload** when the content is stable and approved: a signed-off policy, a finished brand guide, a published price list for this quarter. You want Claude to use *exactly that version*.
- **Connect** when the content changes often or lives in a system of record: a shared planning doc the team edits daily, or your inbox. You want Claude to see *what is true now*.
- **Do not connect 'just in case'.** A connector widens what Claude can see. If a task only needs one document, add that document.

## How connectors work (in plain terms)

The diagram for this lesson shows the architecture underneath connectors. Claude (the host app) talks to a connector, which talks to the outside service. Connectors to common workplace services are the ones you set up yourself by signing in. Connecting Claude to your own internal systems is different: that takes a **custom integration**, typically built by technical staff, sometimes using the **Model Context Protocol (MCP)**, a protocol for connecting AI applications to external tools and data. As an Associate you don't need to build one. You need to know they exist, what they can reach, and that building a **custom connector** to an internal system is more complex, technical work to hand to a Claude Developer or Architect.

## Google Drive and Gmail at a glance

| Connector | What it connects Claude to | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **Google Drive** | Documents and files stored in Drive | Working from current team documents instead of stale copies |
| **Gmail** | Your mailbox | Finding, reading and summarising email threads |

Exactly what a connector can read or do — and which actions require your approval before they run — depends on the service, the plan and organisational policy, and it changes over time. Check Anthropic's current documentation before relying on a specific action.

## Permissions and organisational control

Three ideas matter most:

1. **A connector works through your account.** You sign in to connect a service, and the connection is tied to that account. Treat any connection as giving Claude real access to data in that service, and connect only what the task needs.
2. **The organisation is in control.** Plan settings and organisational policy can restrict which connectors are available and which actions need approval. Follow your organisation's AI policies and governance standards rather than working around them.
3. **Connected services are third parties.** Data that flows through a connector is processed by that service on its own infrastructure under its own terms. That is a governance point: only connect services your organisation has approved, and apply the same data-sensitivity judgment you would before uploading a file.

## Managing connectors day to day

- **Be deliberate about what is connected.** Enable connectors for the conversations and tasks that need them; leave the rest off. If a task only needs one document, you do not need the connector at all.
- **Review and disconnect.** Periodically review which services are connected and disconnect anything you no longer use.
- **Approve actions deliberately.** When a connector-based action needs your sign-off, read what Claude is about to do before approving. Approval steps only protect you if someone actually checks.

## Managing uploaded knowledge

Uploaded files need **you** to keep them fresh:
- Replace a file when the source changes. Delete the old version rather than keeping both.
- Prefer the authoritative document over a summary or a forwarded copy.
- Redact or anonymise sensitive data before uploading, following your organisation's policy — regulated personal identifiers come out first.
- Keep a short list (or a note in the Project) of what is uploaded and when it was last checked.

## Worked example: a marketing operations team

*Situation:* The team runs a weekly campaign status update. Inputs are a campaign plan (a Google Doc edited daily by five people), the approved brand guide (a PDF that changes twice a year) and stakeholder emails.

| Input | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Campaign plan | **Google Drive connector**, pointing at the Doc | Changes daily. A snapshot would be stale by Tuesday |
| Brand guide | **Upload the approved PDF** to the Project | Stable and approved. You want exactly this version |
| Stakeholder emails | **Gmail connector, used only for the status task** | Needed to summarise requests. Anything that gets sent is reviewed by a person first |

What the team does *not* do: connect every available service to every chat, or let a status update go out without a person reading it first.

## Quick decision rules

1. Stable and approved → **upload**.
2. Changes often, or lives in a system of record → **connect**.
3. Needs to *act* (send, create, share) → connector with **approval on and a human in the loop**.
4. Internal system with no ready-made connector → ask a **Developer or Architect** about a custom connector. Don't copy-paste exports around forever.
5. Not approved by your organisation → **don't connect it**, whatever the convenience.
keyTakeaways: Uploaded files are snapshots you maintain by hand. Connectors let Claude work with current content in a service and, for some connectors, take actions.
Upload stable, approved documents. Connect content that changes often or lives in a system of record.
A connector works through your account and gives Claude real access to data in that service — connect only what the task and your policy allow.
Plan settings and organisational policy govern which connectors are available and which actions need approval; follow them.
Connected services process data on their own infrastructure under their own terms, so connect only organisation-approved services.
Custom connectors to internal systems are more complex, technical work for a Developer or Architect.
examTips: If the stem stresses 'the document changes every day' or 'always the latest version', the answer points to a connector, not a fresh upload each time.
If the stem stresses 'the approved version' or 'this quarter's signed-off figures', an uploaded file is usually right.
When an action (sending, sharing, deleting) is involved, prefer the option that keeps a human approving and reviewing.
Governance-flavoured items reward following organisational policy — anonymising regulated data, using only approved services, escalating when unsure — over the most convenient option.
commonTraps: Treating a connector as a small thing. Connecting a service gives Claude access to data in it — scope connections to what the task actually needs.
Assuming an uploaded file updates itself when the original changes.
Connecting every available service to every chat 'for convenience', which widens exposure for no benefit.
Approving connector actions without reading what Claude is about to do.
Building workarounds (exporting and re-uploading daily) instead of asking for a proper connector.
Connecting an unapproved third-party service because a colleague recommended it.

lessons.title: Writing effective system-level instructions
lessons.eli5: System instructions are like the first-day briefing you give a new employee: who they work for, who the customers are, how to sound, and the few things they must never do. A good briefing is short and clear. A bad one is a long list of contradictions nobody could follow.
lessons.body:
## What "system-level" means for an Associate

In everyday Claude use, "system-level instructions" are the **standing instructions that shape every response**, as opposed to the request you type in a single message. In claude.ai, it helps to think in three layers:

| Layer | Where you set it | Applies to | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Account-wide instructions** | Your personal settings | **All** your chats | Personal preferences: "Use UK spelling", "I work in public-sector procurement", "Keep answers concise" |
| **Project instructions** | Inside a Project | Only chats **in that project** | The job: role, audience, format, rules for this body of work |
| **Skills** | Enabled Skills | Loaded **when relevant** to the task | Packaged, repeatable know-how (for example a reporting format or a brand template) with instructions and resources |

The rule of thumb: **put each instruction at the narrowest layer where it is always true.** "Use UK spelling" is true everywhere, so it goes account-wide. "Cite the policy section" is true only for the HR Q&A project, so it goes in that project.

Memory (where enabled) is different. It is what Claude *learns* from past chats, not what you *instruct*. Don't rely on memory to enforce a rule. Write the rule down.

## The anatomy of a strong instruction set

The visual for this lesson breaks a prompt into parts. Standing instructions use the same parts:

1. **Role and purpose.** Who Claude is helping and why. *"You help the customer success team draft replies to renewal questions."*
2. **Audience.** Who reads the output. *"Replies go to finance directors at mid-sized companies."*
3. **Tone and style.** *"Professional, warm, plain English. No jargon or exclamation marks."*
4. **Output format.** *"Two short paragraphs. Greeting, answer, one clear next step, sign-off."*
5. **Use of knowledge.** *"Base pricing answers only on the current Price Sheet in this project."*
6. **What to do when information is missing.** *"If the answer isn't in the documents, say you'll confirm and flag it for a human. Do not guess."*
7. **Hard rules.** *"Never promise discounts. Never mention other customers by name."*

Number 6 is the one people most often forget, and it prevents the most damage. Without it, Claude tends to fill the gap with a plausible answer.

## Worked example: before and after

**Before** (a real-world style first attempt):

> You are an amazing world-class assistant. Be helpful and detailed but also brief. Use the attached files. Be creative! Always be accurate. Write in a friendly but formal tone. Don't make mistakes.

Problems: flattery adds nothing; "detailed but brief" and "friendly but formal" contradict each other; "use the attached files" doesn't say *for what*; "don't make mistakes" is not something Claude can act on; nothing covers missing information.

**After:**

> You help our facilities team answer staff questions about office moves.
> Audience: all employees, many non-technical.
> Tone: clear, calm and friendly. Short paragraphs.
> Format: a direct answer in two or three sentences, then any dates or steps as a short list.
> Facts: use only the Office Move FAQ and the Move Timeline in this project. Mention which one you used.
> If the documents don't answer the question, say so and suggest emailing facilities. Do not guess dates.
> Never share individual employees' desk assignments.

Each line is specific, checkable and free of contradictions.

## Principles that make instructions work

- **Be specific and positive.** "Write in short paragraphs of two to three sentences" beats "don't write long walls of text".
- **Explain the why for important rules.** "Don't include prices, because prices change monthly and the sales team owns them" helps Claude handle cases you didn't foresee.
- **Keep them short.** Every line competes for attention. If an instruction never changes the output, delete it.
- **Set length in sentences or paragraphs, not word counts.** Claude counts tokens, not words, so "two short paragraphs" holds better than "under 150 words".
- **Don't duplicate the knowledge base.** Don't paste the whole style guide into the instructions *and* upload it. Point to the file: "Follow the Brand Voice Guide for tone".
- **Remove contradictions**, including across layers. If your account-wide instructions say "always use bullet points" and the project says "write flowing prose", outputs will be inconsistent. Fix the conflict, don't hope Claude picks right.
- **Use examples sparingly.** One short sample of the desired format often works better than a paragraph describing it.
- **Separate standing rules from task requests.** "Summarise this week's tickets" belongs in a message. "Summaries must list the top three themes first" belongs in instructions.

## Instructions are guidance, not guarantees

Standing instructions make the right behaviour **much more likely**. They do not make it certain. For anything with real consequences (legal wording, numbers going to customers, personal data) keep **human review** in the workflow. The exam often offers "add a stronger instruction" as an option when the real need is a review step or a policy control.

## A quick quality checklist

Before saving instructions, ask:

- Could a new colleague follow these without asking me a question?
- Is every line true for **every** chat at this layer?
- Is there a rule for **missing information**?
- Are there any two lines that pull in opposite directions?
- Is anything here already in a knowledge file?
- Have I tested them with a few real questions?
keyTakeaways: Account-wide instructions apply to all chats, project instructions apply only inside that project, and Skills add packaged capabilities that load when relevant.
Put each instruction at the narrowest layer where it is always true.
Strong instructions cover role, audience, tone, format, how to use knowledge, what to do when information is missing, and a few hard rules.
Keep instructions short, specific, positive and free of contradictions, including contradictions between layers.
Point to knowledge files instead of copying their content into instructions.
Instructions shape behaviour but don't guarantee it. High-stakes output still needs human review.
examTips: If a preference should apply everywhere (spelling, personal role), pick account-wide instructions. If it belongs to one body of work, pick project instructions.
The best rewrite option usually adds audience, format and a rule for missing information, not more adjectives like 'accurate' or 'world-class'.
When outputs are inconsistent across chats, look for contradictory instructions (within or across layers) before blaming the model.
If the stem involves legal, financial or customer-facing risk, an option that relies only on 'tell Claude to be careful' is usually a distractor.
commonTraps: Vague quality words ('be accurate', 'don't make mistakes') that Claude cannot act on.
Contradictory pairs like 'detailed but brief' or 'friendly but formal' with no tie-breaker.
Putting project-specific rules in account-wide instructions, so they leak into unrelated chats.
Pasting an entire style guide into instructions as well as uploading it as knowledge.
Relying on memory to enforce a rule instead of writing the rule into instructions.
Treating a strongly worded instruction as a guarantee for high-stakes output.

lessons.title: Maintaining and updating configurations, knowledge and instructions
lessons.eli5: A Project is like a shop window. It looked great on launch day, but if prices change and nobody updates the tags, shoppers get told the wrong price — very politely and with total confidence. Someone has to own the window, check it on a schedule and fix the tags.
lessons.body:
## Why configuration goes stale

A Project that worked well in January can give wrong answers by June without anyone touching it. The world changed and the configuration didn't:

- A policy was updated, but the old PDF is still in the knowledge base.
- A new price list was uploaded **next to** the old one, so Claude sees two conflicting numbers.
- The team's audience changed (from internal staff to customers), but the instructions still say "internal".
- Someone added a quick rule to fix one bad answer, and it now clashes with an older rule.

The dangerous part: **Claude answers from stale knowledge just as confidently as from current knowledge.** Nothing in the response warns you. Maintenance is how you prevent confidently outdated answers.

## The maintenance loop

Think of it as four repeating steps.

| Step | What you do | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Inform** | Tell people what the configuration is for, what it contains and its limits | A short "About this project" note: purpose, sources, owner, last reviewed date |
| **2. Monitor** | Watch for signals that something is off | User reports, answers citing an old figure, a source document changing |
| **3. Update** | Replace knowledge, refine instructions, adjust connectors | Remove Leave-Policy-2025, add Leave-Policy-2026, update the instruction that mentions it |
| **4. Verify** | Re-test with known questions and compare | Ask the same five benchmark questions and check the answers changed as expected |

Then repeat on a schedule and whenever a trigger fires.

## Triggers that should prompt an update

- A **source document changes** (new policy version, new prices, new org chart).
- **Users report** a wrong or outdated answer.
- The **audience or purpose** of the project changes.
- A **connector** is added, removed, or its permissions change.
- The **organisation's AI policy** changes (for example, new rules on what data can be uploaded).
- Claude product features change in a way that affects how the project is used.

## Good practices

### Ownership and schedule
- Give every shared project a **named owner** (and a backup). "Everyone" maintaining it means no one does.
- Set a **review cadence** that matches how fast the content changes: monthly for a pricing helper, quarterly for a style guide project.
- Limit **who can edit** the project to the owners. Everyone else reports problems rather than making changes themselves.

### One source of truth
- **Replace, don't append.** When a document is superseded, delete the old one. Keeping both is a common cause of inconsistent answers.
- For fast-changing material, consider a **connector to a live source such as Google Drive** rather than uploads you must refresh by hand.
- Avoid copying the same fact into both instructions and knowledge. If it's in both, you have to update it twice, and one copy will eventually be forgotten.

### Change records
- Keep a short **change log**: date, what changed, why, who changed it. It can live in a small document in the project or in your team's usual tracker.
- Record **why** a rule was added. Six months later, "Never mention the legacy plan" makes sense only if someone wrote down that the legacy plan was withdrawn.

### Test before and after
- Keep a small **benchmark set**: five to ten questions with known correct answers, covering the main tasks and at least one "the documents don't cover this" case.
- Run it **before** a change (to know the baseline) and **after** (to confirm the fix and catch side effects).
- Change **one thing at a time** where you can. If you rewrite the instructions and swap three files at once, you can't tell which change helped or hurt.

### Keep instructions lean
Rules accumulate. Every few months, read the instructions top to bottom and ask whether each line is still true, still needed and not contradicted elsewhere. Remove patches that no longer apply.

## Worked example: the out-of-date onboarding helper

*Situation:* A Learning & Development team runs an onboarding Project for new starters. A new hire says Claude told them the probation period is six months, but it was changed to three months last quarter.

**Diagnosis:**
1. Check the knowledge base. Both "Employee-Handbook-2025" and "Employee-Handbook-2026" are present. The old version was never removed.
2. Check the instructions. They say "Use the Employee Handbook". That doesn't say which one.

**Fix:**
1. Remove the 2025 handbook.
2. Leave the instructions pointing to "the Employee Handbook" (now there is only one), and add: "If a new starter's question concerns contract terms, recommend they confirm with HR."
3. Run the benchmark questions, including the probation question. Confirm the answer is now three months.
4. Log the change: date, "removed superseded 2025 handbook", owner.
5. **Inform** users: a short message that the helper was corrected and the probation period is three months, so anyone who acted on the wrong answer can follow up.

**What not to do:** add an instruction saying "the probation period is three months" while leaving both handbooks in place. That patches one symptom, adds a second copy of a fact to maintain, and leaves every other outdated section of the 2025 handbook active.

## Telling people what changed

"Inform" is part of the task statement for a reason. When a shared configuration changes in a way that affects answers, tell the people who use it: what changed, from when, and whether earlier answers might have been wrong. For high-impact errors (pay, contracts, compliance), make sure affected people know rather than quietly fixing it.
keyTakeaways: Stale knowledge produces confidently outdated answers with no warning, so configurations need active maintenance.
Run a loop: inform, monitor, update, verify. Repeat on a schedule and when a trigger fires.
Replace superseded files instead of appending new versions alongside old ones.
Give each shared configuration a named owner, a review cadence and a short change log that records what changed and why.
Keep a small benchmark set of known questions and re-run it before and after every change.
Tell users when a change affects answers, especially if earlier answers may have been wrong.
examTips: When Claude gives an outdated answer in a Project, the first thing to check is the knowledge base for superseded or duplicate files.
Prefer the root-cause fix (remove or replace the stale source) over a patch instruction that hard-codes one corrected fact.
Options that include testing with known questions after a change usually beat options that change things and move on.
If an option names an owner and a review schedule, it often addresses the 'maintain' part of the question better than a one-time fix.
commonTraps: Uploading the new version next to the old one and assuming Claude will pick the newer file.
Patching a single wrong answer with a new instruction while the stale source stays in place.
Changing several things at once, so you can't tell which change fixed or broke something.
Fixing the configuration silently when users may already have acted on wrong answers.
Letting anyone edit a shared project, so nobody owns accuracy.
Assuming that because a project worked at launch, it still works now.

resources.title: Anthropic Partner Academy – Claude Certified Associate prep path (Module 5: Configuration & Knowledge Management)

lessons.title: Configuration drill: Projects, knowledge, connectors and instructions
lessons.eli5: Configuration questions are like deciding where to keep things at home. Daily rules go on the fridge (instructions), reference papers go in the binder (knowledge), and the live calendar stays on the wall (connector). Most wrong answers put the right thing in the wrong place, or forget to throw out last year's papers.
lessons.body:
## How Domain 5 questions are built

Domain 5 (Configuration and Knowledge Management) is worth about 12% of the exam, roughly seven of the 60 items. They are short workplace situations, and most of them test one of four decisions:

1. **Where does this belong?** System-level (account-wide) instructions, project instructions, project knowledge, a connector or just a message.
2. **Upload or connect?** A stable snapshot or the live source.
3. **Is this instruction any good?** Specific, scoped, consistent and covering missing information.
4. **What is the root cause of the bad answer?** Usually stale, duplicate or missing knowledge, or conflicting instructions, rather than "the model".

Use the elimination funnel from the visual: **find the constraint, strip the disguises, pick the fix at the right layer.**

## Distractor families in this domain

| Family | Looks like | Why it's usually wrong |
|---|---|---|
| Paste it every time | "Copy the style guide into each new chat" | Repetitive and error-prone. A Project exists for this |
| Upload everything | "Add the whole shared drive so Claude has full context" | Irrelevant and stale files lower answer quality and widen data exposure |
| Patch the symptom | "Add an instruction stating the correct figure" | Leaves the stale source in place |
| Stronger wording | "Write the rule in capitals and say it's critical" | Doesn't fix a conflict or a missing source, and isn't a guarantee |
| Wrong layer | "Put the project's citation rule in account-wide instructions" | Leaks into unrelated chats |
| Over-connect | "Enable every connector for every chat" | Widens access for no benefit |
| Bypass governance | "Connect the tool yourself, since the owner hasn't enabled it yet" | Workarounds with personal accounts bypass organisational control of work data; connector enablement should go through the workspace owner/admin |
| Blame the model | "Switch to a more capable model" | Doesn't fix bad configuration |

## Drill 1: the repeated brief

*Setup:* A communications officer writes three press releases a week. Each time she pastes the house style rules and the organisation boilerplate into a new chat, and still sometimes forgets a rule.

- **Constraint:** the same context is reused often and must be applied consistently.
- **Disguises:** save the rules in a text file to paste faster; switch to a more capable model; turn on memory and hope Claude remembers.
- **Right layer:** a **Project** with the style rules as project instructions (or a pointer to an uploaded style guide) and the boilerplate as knowledge.

## Drill 2: the stale price

*Setup:* A sales enablement Project answers questions about pricing. After the July price change, Claude sometimes quotes old prices. The knowledge base contains "Pricing-Q2" and "Pricing-Q3".

- **Constraint:** answers must reflect current pricing.
- **Disguises:** add "always use the newest file" to instructions; add an instruction listing the new prices; regenerate until the answer is right.
- **Right layer:** **remove the superseded Pricing-Q2 file**, then re-test with known pricing questions and log the change.

## Drill 3: live doc or upload?

*Setup:* A project manager wants Claude to summarise progress from a delivery tracker that the team edits in Google Docs every day.

- **Constraint:** the content changes daily.
- **Disguises:** download and upload the doc each morning; paste the tracker into instructions.
- **Right layer:** **connect, don't re-upload.** Use the Google Drive connector (or add the doc from Google Drive) so Claude works from the current version rather than yesterday's snapshot.

## Drill 4: the connector that isn't there

*Setup:* In the team's Claude workspace, a coordinator can't find the Gmail connector. A colleague suggests connecting a personal Gmail account instead.

- **Constraint:** work data is governed by organisational policy.
- **Disguises:** the personal-account workaround; forwarding emails into chats in bulk.
- **Right layer:** ask the **workspace owner/admin** to enable the connector through your organisation's approval process, so access follows policy. No workarounds.

## Drill 5: the inconsistent tone

*Setup:* In one Project, some replies come out in bullet points and others as prose. The project instructions say "write in flowing paragraphs". The user's account-wide instructions say "always use bullet points".

- **Constraint:** consistent format in this project.
- **Disguises:** add "IMPORTANT" to the project rule; start a new chat every time.
- **Right layer:** **resolve the conflict.** Move the bullet-point preference out of account-wide instructions, or narrow it so it doesn't apply here.

## Drill 6: the instruction rewrite

*Setup:* Project instructions read "Be helpful, accurate and professional. Use the files." Answers sometimes invent policy details.

- **Constraint:** no invented details.
- **Best rewrite adds:** audience, format, which files to use for which questions, and **what to do when the files don't cover the question** ("say so and refer to the policy team"). Plus human review for anything going to customers.

## Quick-fire

| Stem clue | Answer pattern |
|---|---|
| Same context pasted into many chats | Build a Project |
| Preference true for all your chats | Account-wide (system-level) instructions |
| Rule true only for one workstream | Project instructions |
| Packaged, repeatable know-how used across contexts | A Skill |
| Approved, stable document | Upload as project knowledge |
| Changes daily or lives in a system of record | Connector (e.g., Google Drive) for the live source |
| Connector missing in your workspace | Owner/admin enables it — never a personal-account workaround |
| Claude needs to send or share things | Connector, with a human reviewing outgoing actions |
| Outdated answer in a Project | Look for stale or duplicate files first |
| After any change | Re-run known test questions |
| Shared Project, several colleagues | Keep instruction changes controlled and reviewed |
| Internal system with no connector | Hand off to a Claude Developer (custom integration) |

## Final checklist before you answer

- Is the information **stable or changing**? (Upload vs connect.)
- Is the rule **always true at this layer**? (Account vs project vs Skill.)
- Does the fix address the **source** of the bad answer, not just one symptom?
- Does the option respect **permissions and organisational control**?
- Is there a **test or review step** where the stakes call for one?
keyTakeaways: Most Domain 5 questions ask where something belongs, whether to upload or connect, whether an instruction is well written, or what caused a bad answer.
Stale or duplicate knowledge and conflicting instructions are the usual root causes, not the model.
Fix at the right layer: Project for reuse, account-wide instructions for universal preferences, connector for live data, and organisational approval — not workarounds — for governed connectors.
Re-test with known questions after every configuration change.
examTips: Classify each option by layer (message, account instructions, project instructions, knowledge, connector, governance) before judging it.
Eliminate options that only make wording stronger when the stem describes a conflict or a stale source.
Eliminate workarounds that bypass organisational governance or unapproved services, even if they would 'work'.
When two options both fix the problem, prefer the one that also keeps a single source of truth.
commonTraps: Choosing 'switch to a more capable model' for what is really a configuration problem.
Choosing the upload-everything option because 'more context is better'.
Choosing a patch instruction over removing the stale file.
Choosing a personal-account or unapproved workaround when a connector isn't enabled.
